summary: A draft plan, written by Vint Cerf and Jon Postel, for moving computer mail from the old ARPANET protocols to the new Internet protocols. It aims to keep mail working and minimize the impact on users while both sets of protocols are in use.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 771 lays out how computer mail could continue to move while hosts changed from ARPANET protocols to Internet protocols. It relies on mailers choosing direct delivery or a relay based on the destination host's capabilities.

subtitle: A plan for keeping mail working while switching from ARPANET to Internet protocols.

tldr.problem: Mail had to move between the ARPANET's NCP environment and the Internet's TCP environment without disrupting users or existing mail software.
tldr.mechanism: Mailers use host capability tables to decide whether to deliver directly or send through a relay host that supports both environments.
tldr.outcome: The memo sets out a transition plan for text mail and its connectivity cases; it explicitly does not cover the later move to multimedia mail.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 771's status as Unknown. The RFC identifies itself as a draft memo and requests comments.

sections.title: What the Transition Covers
sections.content:
The plan aims to preserve equivalent or better mail service while the ARPANET and Internet protocol environments overlap. It focuses on moving text mail between the older ARPANET environment, which uses NCP, and the Internet environment, which uses TCP.

The memo limits its scope to that transition. It does not address a later change from text-only mail to multimedia mail.
sections.plainLanguage: The plan covers keeping text email working during a change in network protocols. It does not cover adding multimedia to mail.

sections.title: Relays and Host Capability Tables
sections.content:
A mailer must determine whether it can reach the destination directly using its available communication system. If not, it selects a mail relay host that connects the NCP and TCP environments.

An expanded host table maps names to Internet addresses and includes flags describing whether a host uses old-table NCP, new-table NCP, TCP, or another kind of connection. When a message goes through a relay, the transfer information includes the destination host; an origin address allows the relay to report later delivery errors.
sections.plainLanguage: The sending mailer checks what protocols the destination can use. If direct delivery is not possible, it sends the message to a relay that can continue the trip.

sections.title: How the Nine Delivery Cases Differ
sections.content:
The memo compares exchanges among old-table NCP hosts, new-table NCP hosts, and TCP hosts. Some pairs can exchange mail directly, while exchanges across protocol boundaries need a relay; the transfer may use the older file-transfer method or the newer mail-transfer protocol.

For example, TCP-to-TCP delivery is direct over TCP using the mail-transfer protocol. An old-table NCP host sending to a TCP host requires a special relay because the old host does not include the destination host in the transfer command.
sections.plainLanguage: Hosts using the same mail arrangements can often send directly. When their arrangements differ, a relay translates the path between them.

sections.title: Keeping Mail Readers and Replies Working
sections.content:
The plan aims to minimize changes to programs that compose and read mail. A program that checks host names may need the expanded host table, and message headers should include both mailbox and host so replies remain correctly addressed after relaying.

Relay servers may accept a message before confirming that its final mailbox is reachable. The plan therefore calls for enough origin information to return a later error and for the relay to include the full message in that error report.
sections.plainLanguage: Complete mailbox and host addresses help reply programs keep working when mail passes through a relay. The relay also needs the sender's address to report a delivery failure.
